---
title: "Forecasting US Industrial Production"
subtitle: "SARIMA, exponential smoothing and a VAR with consumer sentiment"
execute:
  freeze: false  # always re-read the results saved by the analysis pages
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/setup.R")

# Results saved by univariate.qmd and multivariate.qmd
uni <- readRDS("results/univariate.rds")
mv <- readRDS("results/multivariate.rds")

f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)

# Rolling-origin results
cv_rmse_1 <- uni$cv_1[, "RMSE"]
cv_rmse_12 <- uni$cv_12[, "RMSE"]
stat_models <- c("SARIMA", "ETS", "Holt-Winters")
naive_lower_from <- min(uni$sarima_last_better, uni$ets_last_better) + 1
naive_p_after <- uni$naive_p[naive_lower_from:nrow(uni$naive_p), ]

# Out-of-sample value of sentiment
cw_p <- mv$cw_table[["p-value (one-sided)"]]

# Outlook
fut <- uni$future
fut_last <- fut[nrow(fut), ]
```

This project forecasts the monthly **US Industrial Production Index**
(1990–2025) and tests whether **consumer sentiment** helps to anticipate it. It
compares classical time series models on a held-out test period, from data
preparation and statistical testing to model diagnostics and a rolling-origin
backtest.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ip
#| fig-cap: "US industrial production, total index (2017 = 100, not seasonally adjusted)"
autoplot(ip_ts) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Index (2017 = 100)")
```

## Key findings

- **The series needs transforming before modelling.** Industrial production has
  a trend, a strong seasonal pattern and two large shocks (2008–2009 and 2020).
  Unit root tests (KPSS, ADF, Phillips-Perron) agree that it is non-stationary;
  the HEGY test shows a stochastic trend (p = `r f2(uni$hegy_t1_p)`) but a
  deterministic seasonal pattern (seasonal unit roots rejected, p < 0.01).
- **No model clearly wins.** With a single forecast origin (June 2016), SARIMA
  looked best (RMSE `r f2(uni$single_origin["SARIMA", "RMSE"])`). A
  rolling-origin evaluation, which re-estimates the models every month, is more
  reliable: SARIMA, ETS and Holt-Winters are statistically tied one month ahead
  (RMSE `r f2(min(cv_rmse_1[stat_models]))`–`r f2(max(cv_rmse_1[stat_models]))`)
  and all significantly beat a seasonal naive benchmark
  (`r f2(cv_rmse_1["Seasonal naive"])`). From about `r naive_lower_from` months
  ahead the seasonal naive forecast has a lower RMSE, but the difference is not
  statistically significant at any horizon (Diebold-Mariano p ≥ `r floor(100 * min(naive_p_after)) / 100`).
- **Consumer sentiment has statistically significant but small predictive
  content.** The two series are not cointegrated. In a VAR with seasonal
  dummies, sentiment Granger-causes industrial production
  (p = `r sprintf("%.3f", mv$granger_umc_p)`) but not the reverse
  (p = `r f2(mv$granger_ipb_p)`), and it explains about
  `r round(100 * mv$fevd_10["IPB_d", "UMCSENT_d"])`% of production's forecast
  variance. A typical sentiment shock (about `r round(mv$shock_size)` points)
  raises the production index by about
  `r f1(min(mv$cum_irf_12))`–`r f1(max(mv$cum_irf_12))` points over a year.
  Adding sentiment to the model **does not improve out-of-sample forecasts**:
  neither the Diebold-Mariano test nor the Clark-West test for nested models
  finds a gain (Clark-West one-sided p between `r f2(min(cw_p))` and
  `r f2(max(cw_p))`).
- **Outlook:** a SARIMA model re-estimated on all data forecasts the index at
  around `r round(min(fut$forecast))`–`r round(max(fut$forecast))`
  through `r fut_last$month` (95% interval `r round(fut_last$lower95)`–`r round(fut_last$upper95)`).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Rolling-origin RMSE in index points, forecasts made every month from June 2016 to March 2025"
summary_models <- c("SARIMA", "ETS", "Holt-Winters", "Seasonal naive")
data.frame(
  Model = c(paste0(uni$sarima_spec, ", log"), uni$ets_spec, "Holt-Winters, additive",
            "Seasonal naive (benchmark)"),
  `1 month ahead` = f2(cv_rmse_1[summary_models]),
  `12 months ahead` = f2(cv_rmse_12[summary_models]),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-outlook
#| tbl-cap: "Industrial production forecast (index, 2017 = 100), SARIMA estimated on January 1990 to April 2025"
data.frame(
  Month = fut$month,
  `SARIMA forecast` = f1(fut$forecast),
  `95% interval` = paste(f1(fut$lower95), "–", f1(fut$upper95)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

**Takeaway:** one month ahead, any of the three statistical models clearly
beats a naive benchmark; from about `r naive_lower_from` months ahead a naive
seasonal forecast has lower errors, although not significantly, so the models
add clear value only at the shortest horizon. Consumer sentiment helps at the
margin in sample, but not enough to improve forecasts.

## Limitations

- **Prediction intervals are probably too narrow in crises.** Model residuals
  show ARCH effects (volatility clustering) and heavy tails, while the
  intervals assume constant, normal errors.
- **The pandemic dominates the errors.** A few months in 2020 produce the
  largest forecast errors; results excluding them are reported as a robustness
  check, and the main conclusions do not change.
- **Revised data, not real-time data.** The backtest uses the data as revised
  by December 2025, not the figures available to a forecaster at each date.
- **One series and one sample.** The conclusions apply to this index and this
  period.
- **Seasonal differencing is a modelling choice.** The HEGY test points to
  deterministic seasonality; a model with a first difference and monthly
  dummies was not tested as a forecasting alternative to SARIMA.

## How the analysis is organised

- [**Univariate models**](univariate.qmd): visual analysis, stationarity and
  seasonality tests, ARMA, SARIMA, ETS, Holt-Winters, a seasonal naive
  benchmark, residual diagnostics, single-origin and rolling-origin
  evaluation, and the forecast to 2028.
- [**VAR analysis**](multivariate.qmd): consumer sentiment, Johansen
  cointegration test, VAR with seasonal dummies, Granger causality, impulse
  responses, variance decomposition, an out-of-sample test of the value of
  sentiment (Diebold-Mariano and Clark-West) and a 24-month forecast.

## Data

| Series | Description | Source |
|---|---|---|
| IPB50001N | Industrial Production: Total Index, 2017 = 100, not seasonally adjusted | Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, via FRED |
| UMCSENT | University of Michigan: Consumer Sentiment, 1966:Q1 = 100 | Surveys of Consumers, University of Michigan, via FRED |

Monthly data from January 1990 to April 2025 (`r uni$n_obs` observations),
retrieved from ALFRED using the vintage of 17 December 2025 so that the results
can be reproduced exactly. See the
[data notes](https://github.com/xwmara/us-industrial-production-forecast/tree/main/data)
for citations and terms of use.

## Tools

R (forecast, urca, tseries, uroot, lmtest, FinTS, vars, sandwich), Quarto for
the report and renv for package versions.

## About

This is a portfolio adaptation of a team project for the Time Series course at
the Bucharest University of Economic Studies (2025). The analysis was reviewed
and extended for this version: the forecast evaluation, the VAR specification
and several tests were corrected, and an out-of-sample test of consumer
sentiment was added. See the
[README](https://github.com/xwmara/us-industrial-production-forecast#credits)
for credits.
